facts.t: The man who lost his case saved the Constitution
facts.d: Kesavananda Bharati was the head of the Edneer Mutt in Kerala, challenging state land-reform laws that affected his mutt's property. He effectively lost on the facts — the land reforms survived — yet the judgment delivered in his name became India's most important constitutional decision.

The Kesavananda hearing remains the longest in Supreme Court history. The judgment runs past 700 pages with eleven separate opinions, and the operative summary was signed by only nine of the thirteen judges — several later disputed what they had signed.

Courts in Bangladesh, Pakistan, Uganda, Belize and Kenya have cited Kesavananda in developing their own limits on amending power. A doctrine with no textual home in the Indian Constitution has become one of India's most influential legal exports.

bank.q: The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) was decided by a bench of:
bank.e: Thirteen judges — still the largest bench ever constituted by the Supreme Court of India. Coelho (2007), often confused with it, was nine.

bank.q: Which one of the following statements about the origins of the Basic Structure Doctrine is NOT correct?
o: It was influenced by radical constitutional amendments in Weimar Germany
The German professor Conrad is credited with the genesis of the idea
It was first laid down authoritatively in Shankari Prasad (1951)
Nani Palkhivala is credited with persuading the Supreme Court to formulate it
bank.e: Shankari Prasad went the other way — it held that Parliament's constituent power was unlimited. The doctrine was mentioned briefly in Golak Nath (1967) and cemented in Kesavananda (1973).

bank.as: The Basic Structure Doctrine rests on the theory of implied limitation.
bank.rs: The Constitution expressly lists the features that cannot be amended.
bank.e: The Assertion is true; the Reason is false. There is no eternity clause in the Indian Constitution — the limitation is implied by the courts from the document's structure, which is exactly why critics call the doctrine judge-made.

bank.q: Consider the following criticisms of the Basic Structure Doctrine:
s: It finds no mention in the constitutional text.
Its scope is ambiguous and undefined.
It allows unelected judges to veto the amendments of elected majorities.
bank.e: All three are standard criticisms. The third — the counter-majoritarian difficulty — is the sharpest, and it was felt most acutely when the NJAC amendment was struck down.

bank.q: Who described the Basic Structure Doctrine as a north star which guides the interpreters and implementers of the Constitution?
bank.e: CJI D. Y. Chandrachud used the north star metaphor — the doctrine gives direction when the constitutional path ahead is convoluted.

bank.q: Match List I (impact of the doctrine) with List II (its content):
pairs: 1. Parliament holds constituent power in trust for the people
2. The Union–State distribution of powers cannot be altered
3. The Court has coextensive power to invalidate offending amendments
4. Progressive interpretation while the core stays protected
bank.e: If Parliament has an unfettered right to amend, the Court claims a coextensive power to review — that is the checks-and-balances point. Trusteeship of constituent power is the constitutionalism point.

bank.q: Which one of the following has NOT been suggested as a possible future route around the Basic Structure Doctrine?
o: Review by a bench larger than thirteen judges
Revolution, as noted by D. D. Basu
bank.e: A referendum route does not exist in Indian constitutional law and has not been part of this debate. The other three — a larger bench, a fresh Constituent Assembly, or revolution in Basu's sense — are the routes actually discussed.

bank.q: Arrange the following in correct chronological order:
items: The doctrine is cemented by a thirteen-judge bench
The doctrine is mentioned briefly in Golak Nath
bank.e: Weimar Germany and Conrad's scholarship → a passing mention in Golak Nath (1967) → full formulation in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

bank.q: The Basic Structure Doctrine is credited with protecting India from the fate of several South Asian neighbours, chiefly by preventing:
o: Totalitarian rule, military coups and extra-constitutional change
bank.e: The domino argument: constitutional entrenchment made self-perpetuating rule far harder in India than in states where amending power was unlimited.

bank.q: With reference to the effect of the doctrine on Fundamental Rights, consider the following:
s: No amendment can dilute or abrogate rights such as equality and free speech.
The doctrine bars all amendments touching Part III.
The doctrine permits progressive expansion of rights while protecting the core.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 overstates it — Part III can be amended; what cannot be done is destruction of the principles underlying those rights. Golak Nath took the absolute position and was overruled.

bank.as: The Basic Structure Doctrine limits amendments without freezing the Constitution.
bank.rs: It distinguishes between abridging a feature and abrogating it.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion. An amendment may curtail or regulate a basic feature; it falls only when the essence is eliminated. This is what keeps the doctrine a bridge rather than a barrier.
